messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Raymond Okafor was a 55-year-old African American man who came to treatment several months after his wife died suddenly, leaving him with a PCL-5 score of 67 and a life that, in his words, no longer felt like his own. The death had been unexpected and traumatic: one evening she had collapsed at home, and by the time the ambulance arrived there was nothing anyone could do. Raymond could still picture the blur of that night in pieces — the hallway light, the stretcher, the flashing emergency lights outside the house — but just as often he was hit by the raw feeling of it without a clear picture at all, a surge of panic and grief that seemed to rise out of nowhere. From the start, ambulance sirens, talk of other people losing loved ones, and even the sight of the workplace where he painted houses were enough to pull him back toward that night. A passing ambulance on the street could make his chest tighten and his thoughts race to his wife; a conversation at work about someone’s mother or brother dying could leave him staring blankly at a wall, overwhelmed by the same grief he felt when he first heard she was gone. He noticed that remembering the event was rarely a calm recollection. The memories came as vivid images — his wife on the floor, the paramedics kneeling beside her, the look on the faces of neighbors gathered outside — and once those images surfaced, he felt emotionally flooded and then immediately on guard, as if danger were still unfolding in front of him.

Over time Raymond came to believe that the trauma had not simply taken his wife but had taken something essential from him as well. He said he did not know himself anymore and felt set apart from other people, especially when coworkers joked about family or spoke casually about the future. That sense that his life had been destroyed sat heavily with him and made ordinary moments feel contaminated by loss. It also sharpened his vigilance. At night, when the house was quiet and his wife’s absence was most obvious, he found it harder to feel safe than during the day; he lay awake listening for sounds from outside, body tense and ready to react, and even inside his own home he felt on guard. He noticed that the more he told himself he was broken and isolated, the more his body stayed braced for danger, as if his mind were warning him that something terrible could happen again at any moment. Those beliefs fed back into the memories too. When he tried to think about his wife, the pictures came quickly, but they were often followed by a blank, unbearable emotional wave that confirmed for him that the loss had shattered him. In those moments he would be flooded with the conviction that his life had been ruined beyond repair.

Raymond also began to manage his distress by avoiding the places and topics that set it off, though the relief never lasted. He started taking different routes to avoid ambulances whenever possible and found himself pulling away from conversations at work that turned to illness, funerals, or other people’s bereavements. At his painting job, which should have kept him busy, he became uneasy around the rhythm of the workplace itself — the noise of engines, the sight of service vehicles pulling up near a site, even the mention of a colleague being late because of an emergency. Each of these moments could spark the same chain: the trigger would bring back the images or the emotional force of his wife’s death, the memories would make him feel exposed and unsafe, and the feeling of being changed and alone would push him to keep his distance from people and places that might remind him of what happened. He gradually spent less time chatting with coworkers and more time working in silence, which only deepened the sense that he was apart from others.

By the time he sought help, Raymond was sleeping poorly, checking the doors at night, and feeling constantly keyed up in a way that made him exhausted and irritable. He described moving through his days with the sense that the world could break open without warning, and that anything connected to ambulances, his work, or stories of loss could drag him back into the most painful parts of that night. What brought him in was the fear that he was becoming unreachable even to himself, and what he most hoped for was some way to feel safe in his own home again without being ambushed by the pictures, the grief, and the certainty that his life had ended when his wife died.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette shows triggers leading to distress, but does not explicitly state that triggers cause a sense of threat.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette links triggers to vivid memories and emotional reactions, but does not clearly state that triggers drive the trauma memory itself.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers prompting distress and reminders of the loss, but does not clearly state that triggers lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette describes negative beliefs increasing vigilance, but does not explicitly state that those appraisals produce threat as a causal effect within one paragraph.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette says beliefs feed back into the memories, but does not clearly state that negative appraisals generate the memory content or intrusion.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly show negative appraisals causing triggers or cue reactivity.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette shows memories making him feel flooded and on guard, but does not clearly state that the memory causes threat as a causal relationship within one paragraph.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette says memories are followed by a conviction that his life was ruined, but does not clearly state that the memory leads to negative appraisals in causal form.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that memories themselves generate triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette says feeling threatened increases guarding, but does not clearly state that threat drives the memory/intrusion process.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows feeling unsafe and on guard, but does not clearly state that threat causes triggers to become activated.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
From the start, ambulance sirens, talk of other people losing loved ones, and even the sight of the workplace where he painted houses were enough to pull him back toward that night. A passing ambulance on the street could make his chest tighten and his thoughts race to his wife; a conversation at work about someone’s mother or brother dying could leave him staring blankly at a wall, overwhelmed by the same grief he felt when he first heard she was gone.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each of those cues did more than upset him: they instantly felt like danger, as if something terrible were about to happen again. The siren on a city street or the sound of a service vehicle arriving at a job site could put him on edge before he had time to think, and the scene at work itself — the noise, the trucks, the talk of emergencies — became a place where threat seemed to follow him in.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The memories came as vivid images — his wife on the floor, the paramedics kneeling beside her, the look on the faces of neighbors gathered outside — and once those images surfaced, he felt emotionally flooded and then immediately on guard, as if danger were still unfolding in front of him.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When those pictures broke through, they did not stay in the past; they pulled him straight back into the room, with the hallway light, the stretcher, and the flashing lights feeling close enough to touch. Afterward, even ordinary sounds and sights around him seemed to carry the same charge, as if the memory had trained him to see warnings everywhere.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time Raymond came to believe that the trauma had not simply taken his wife but had taken something essential from him as well. He said he did not know himself anymore and felt set apart from other people, especially when coworkers joked about family or spoke casually about the future.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once he had settled on that meaning, almost anything could confirm it: a passing ambulance, a question about someone being sick, or even hearing a neighbor mention a funeral would land as proof that the world was unsafe and that he was permanently changed by it. Those appraisals made him feel as though danger was already in the air around him, before anything had actually happened.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He noticed that the more he told himself he was broken and isolated, the more his body stayed braced for danger, as if his mind were warning him that something terrible could happen again at any moment. Those beliefs fed back into the memories too.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Having decided that he was damaged beyond repair, he walked through his days already expecting threat, so new cues stood out sharply and caught hold of him. That same conviction also kept pulling him back to the night his wife died, making the images return with a force that seemed to prove his fear about himself.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When he tried to think about his wife, the pictures came quickly, but they were often followed by a blank, unbearable emotional wave that confirmed for him that the loss had shattered him. In those moments he would be flooded with the conviction that his life had been ruined beyond repair.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time the memory returned, it left him feeling as if the danger were still present, not over and done with, and that immediate sense of threat made the pictures harder to shake. The same intrusion also led him straight back to the thought that he was broken by it and would never be the same man he had been before.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Raymond also began to manage his distress by avoiding the places and topics that set it off, though the relief never lasted. He started taking different routes to avoid ambulances whenever possible and found himself pulling away from conversations at work that turned to illness, funerals, or other people’s bereavements.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The more he had come to see the world as dangerous and himself as unable to cope, the more even small things started to register as warnings — an ambulance heard two blocks away, a remark about a hospital, a neighbor’s car with the lights still on late at night. Those cues kept him scanning, and the scanning made it feel as though threat was always just beneath the surface.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
By the time he sought help, Raymond was sleeping poorly, checking the doors at night, and feeling constantly keyed up in a way that made him exhausted and irritable. He described moving through his days with the sense that the world could break open without warning, and that anything connected to ambulances, his work, or stories of loss could drag him back into the most painful parts of that night.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Even when he was trying to keep busy, the persistent sense of danger kept the memory close, so a siren heard from inside the house or a vehicle pulling up outside his painting job could bring the whole scene back in a flash. Once that happened, the old fear returned with it, making the cue feel even more powerful and harder for him to dismiss the next time.
<<<END>>>
